title: 'Everybody Gets to Choose' — But the Audience Already Has: How Dhurandhar Ended Bollywood's Spy Franchise Debate
excerpt: Anupria Goenka's diplomatic defence of YRF's spy universe can't hide the numbers: Aditya Dhar's two-film franchise has crossed ₹3,000 crore worldwide, and NRIs are its secret growth engine
body:
When Anupria Goenka — who played the sharp, understated Naina in Siddharth Anand's *War* — was asked about Aditya Chopra's spy universe being compared unfavourably to the Dhurandhar franchise, she offered the most diplomatic answer possible: "Everybody gets to choose."

She's right, of course. But the audience has already chosen. And the numbers aren't close.

## The Scoreboard

Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar franchise — two films, both starring Ranveer Singh as RAW operative Jaskirat Singh Rangi — has now grossed over ₹3,000 crore worldwide combined. The first film crossed ₹1,300 crore globally in 2025, making it the biggest Bollywood overseas grosser of the year. The sequel, *Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge*, released on March 19, 2026, surpassed Pushpa 2 to become the third-highest-grossing Indian film worldwide at ₹1,796 crore. In India alone, it has netted ₹1,181 crore — the first Bollywood film ever to breach the ₹1,100 crore mark.

Meanwhile, YRF's spy universe — Tiger, War, Pathaan — has had a rougher recent run. *Tiger 3* underperformed in 2023. *War 2* has been stuck in development. *Pathaan* was a genuine blockbuster, but Aditya Chopra's factory-model approach to franchise filmmaking has started feeling formulaic precisely when Dhurandhar's grittier, R-rated sensibility found its audience.

## What Made the Difference

The distinction isn't subtle. YRF's spy films are glossy, four-quadrant entertainers — designed to sell in single screens and multiplexes alike, packed with songs, dance sequences, and a Tiger Zinda Hai-style "India always wins" simplicity.

Dhurandhar operates differently. Aditya Dhar builds his world through intelligence briefings, surveillance sequences, and a moral ambiguity that treats the audience like adults. There are no item numbers. The violence is unflinching. And the OTT release of *Dhurandhar 2* — a "Raw & Unseen" cut running 229 minutes with restored dialogues and heightened violence — reinforced what the theatrical version only hinted at: this franchise doesn't need to soften itself to sell.

## The NRI Factor

Here's what rarely gets discussed in the spy franchise wars: the diaspora is Dhurandhar's secret growth engine.

The first film earned ₹70 crore in North America alone in its second weekend. The sequel opened day-and-date in international markets and started streaming on Netflix in the US and Canada from May 15 — weeks before India's JioHotstar release on June 4. NRIs didn't just watch it; they drove the uncut version to the top of Netflix's global charts.

There's a reason for this. Dhurandhar's politics — RAW operations in Pakistan, intelligence networks across the Middle East, a protagonist who operates in morally grey territory — resonates with a diaspora that consumes global thrillers like *Sicario* and *Zero Dark Thirty* but wants Indian stories told at that level. YRF's spy films, by contrast, play it safer — which works domestically but limits international upside.

## Where Both Franchises Go Next

Ranveer Singh's next project, *Pralay*, begins filming in August 2026 with a reported ₹300 crore budget, further cementing the Dhurandhar universe. Meanwhile, Aditya Chopra has quietly been developing a Jim spin-off and is reportedly rethinking the tone of his spy films — a tacit acknowledgment that the market has shifted.

Anupria Goenka's defence of YRF's spy universe was gracious. She emphasised that both franchises "get to coexist" and that audiences have room for different kinds of espionage storytelling. She's not wrong. But when one franchise has earned nearly twice what the other has in its best year, "everybody gets to choose" sounds less like a statement of creative diversity and more like a concession speech.

Aditya Dhar didn't just build a spy franchise. He built the one Bollywood didn't know it needed — and, for NRIs craving Hollywood-grade action with Indian souls, the one they'd been waiting for.
